title: Let everything that has breath (Psalm 150)
hook: trumpet, harp, cymbals, dance: the psalter ends in pure praise
carry: your breath goes back as praise

segments.voice: Yesterday, a roll call of sea monsters, snow and children, all in one choir. Your line: a cedar praises by growing like a cedar.
screen: `A CEDAR PRAISES BY GROWING LIKE A CEDAR.`

segments.voice: You've probably said today's word without thinking. Shouted in a gospel choir. Sung by a whole hall standing up in the middle of a Christmas concert. Muttered when the bus finally shows up after twenty minutes in the rain. It's one of a handful of words that have traveled, nearly unchanged, from ancient Hebrew into dozens of languages. And it's the word the book of Psalms ends on. After a hundred and forty-nine psalms of tears, rage, waiting and thanks, the last one has no story and no request. Just instruments, dancing and one word.
screen: `A GOSPEL CHOIR.` → `THE BUS FINALLY COMES.` → `THE LAST WORD OF THE PSALMS.`

segments.voice: Hallelujah is two Hebrew words joined. Hallelu means praise, and it's plural, a command to a crowd: all of you, praise. Yah is a short form of God's own name. So: everybody, praise the Lord. The King James Bible usually translates it rather than spelling it out, which is why Psalm one hundred fifty begins and ends with "Praise ye the LORD." In between, an orchestra. "Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp. Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs. Praise him upon the loud cymbals: praise him upon the high sounding cymbals." The trumpet is likely the shofar, the ram's horn. The timbrel is a hand drum. And organs isn't a pipe organ: in 1611 the word could mean any instrument, and the Hebrew probably means a pipe or flute. The psalm wants it noisy. Then the last line: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Not everything with a voice, or faith, or talent. Everything with breath. The Hebrew word for breath is neshamah, the same word Genesis uses when God breathes the breath of life into the first human. The breath that was given goes back as praise. In the New Testament the word appears only in Revelation, in Greek as alleluia, sung by a great multitude in heaven. Many Western churches stop saying alleluia during Lent and bring it back with joy at Easter; Orthodox Christians keep singing it all year round.
screen: `HALLELU: ALL OF YOU, PRAISE` · `YAH: THE NAME OF GOD` · `SHOFAR, HARP, DRUM, CYMBALS` · `NESHAMAH: THE BREATH OF LIFE` · then, large: `LET EVERY THING THAT HATH BREATH PRAISE THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Notice your breathing; it came in this morning without you asking. Breathe in slowly, and on each out-breath let a word ride out: hallelujah, said softly, if you pray, or thanks, or simply the breath itself as gratitude. In, given; out, given back.
Hallelujah. Hebrew for: all of you, praise the Lord. The last word of the book of Psalms, and one of the most traveled words on earth.
Your line: your breath goes back as praise. A whole book of tears and rage ends right here. Day four hundred forty, done.

howItsDone: Christians sing hallelujah (or alleluia) throughout worship, especially at Easter; many Western churches set it aside during Lent, while Orthodox Christians sing it all year.

chat.says: People shout hallelujah all the time. What does it actually mean?
options: Hebrew: hallelu, all of you praise, and Yah, God's name. Everybody, praise the Lord.
It's Greek for amen, so it means so be it, said at the end of a prayer.
It's a Latin word the church made up for Easter, meaning he is risen.
chat.meaning: Hallelujah joins two Hebrew words: hallelu, a plural command to praise, and Yah, a short form of God's name.

shofar.meaning: a ram's horn, likely the psalm's trumpet

neshamah.meaning: Hebrew for breath, as in God's breath of life

alleluia.meaning: the Greek form of hallelujah, sung in Revelation

Lent.meaning: the season before Easter, when many Western churches stop saying alleluia

notes: Year one day 139 touched Psalm 150:3–6 briefly in a lesson on worship music; this day focuses on the word hallelujah.
Trumpet in 150:3 is shofar in Hebrew. Confirm.
'Organs' (Hebrew 'ugav) probably a pipe or flute. Confirm.
Neshamah in Psalm 150:6 and Genesis 2:7 (nishmat chayyim). Confirm.
Alleluia in the New Testament: Revelation 19:1, 3, 4, 6 only. Confirm.
Lenten 'burying the alleluia' in Western churches (Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and others); Orthodox sing alleluia during Lent (even more prominently at Lenten Matins). Confirm wording.
